content:
Eating less can creep up gradually. With arthritis and frailty, it can make muscles weaker and recovery slower.

This guide covers causes and practical ways to eat enough. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why appetite can drop

  • Pain and fatigue.
  • Some medicines, such as those that cause nausea or a dry mouth.
  • Low mood or loneliness.
  • Difficulty shopping, cooking or opening packaging.
  • Dental or swallowing problems.

Warning signs

  • Clothes, rings or dentures becoming loose.
  • Losing weight without trying.
  • Feeling weak or tired more often.

Practical tips

  • Eat small meals and snacks often.
  • Include protein at each meal.
  • Use nourishing drinks such as milky drinks.
  • Keep easy foods within reach.
  • Eat with others when possible.

Getting help

See your GP about unplanned weight loss. They may check for other causes and refer you to a dietitian. Meal delivery, help with shopping and an OT assessment for kitchen tasks may help.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I take supplements?

Ask your GP or a dietitian before starting nutritional supplements.

Is losing weight good for arthritis?

Planned weight loss can help some people, but unplanned weight loss in frailty is a concern.
